To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the acquisition of a second language is an inherently social process.
the acquisition of a second language is a process of social interaction and learning.

(1) the zone of proximate development, as a construct of sociocultural psychology, provides a framework for the description and analysis of second language acquisition, (2) the concept of egocentric speech provides a framework for describing the discourse of learners in second language contexts, and (3) the notion of the interdependence of language and thought provides a framework for understanding the nature of language learning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which language is used to accomplish various tasks, and the way in which the use of language shapes the way in which we understand the world.
the discursive practices that are used in the process of second language learning.

the ways in which the discursive practices that occur in the zone of proximally development (or in other words, the discursive practices in which the learner is engaged in the process of acquiring a new skill) can be analyzed and understood in terms of the sociocultural context in which those practices occur.

sociocultural theory is the most promising theoretical framework available for research on second language discourse, because it provides the most comprehensive account of language use, language acquisition and language learning, and because it is the most consistent with what we know about human learning and cognition in general.
the study has shown that the use of a sociocultural approach to language learning has been successful in helping students to learn a foreign language.

we are trying to understand the nature of language and language use in the classroom.

it is an attempt to develop a theoretical framework for the study of second language learning and teaching that is consistent with current developments in sociocultural theory, and that is also informed by a number of empirical studies that we have done over the last 15 or 20 years on second language discourse.
